# Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
# install.packages(c("tidyverse","readxl","janitor","gtsummary","gt",
#                     "corrplot","GGally","skimr"))

library(tidyverse)   
library(readxl)      
library(janitor)     
library(gtsummary)   
library(gt)          
library(corrplot)    
library(GGally)      
library(skimr)       
```

# 1. Import and Tidy

## 1b) Import the data

Adjust the path/filename to wherever you saved the file. Use ONE of the
two import lines below depending on whether you have the `.csv` or `.xlsx`
version.

```{r import}
# CSV version
lifestyledata <- read_csv("lifestyle.csv") %>% clean_names()

# XLSX version (uncomment if using Excel file instead)
# lifestyledata <- read_excel("lifestyle.xlsx") %>% clean_names()

glimpse(lifestyledata)
```

`clean_names()` converts columns like "BMI", "Weight (kg)" into consistent
lower_snake_case names (e.g. `bmi`, `weight_kg`). Check `names(lifestyledata)`
after import and adjust the variable names used below (I have used `bmi`,
`age`, `weight`, `id`, `year` as placeholders — rename to match your data).

```{r check-names}
names(lifestyledata)
```

## 1a/c) Structure and missing values

```{r structure}
str(lifestyledata)

# Overview of structure + missingness for every variable
skim(lifestyledata)

# Total missing values across the whole dataset
sum(is.na(lifestyledata))

# Missing values per column
colSums(is.na(lifestyledata))
```

## 1b) Number of subjects

```{r n-subjects}
lifestyledata %>%
  summarise(n_subjects = n_distinct(id))
```

## 1c) Number and list of timepoints

```{r timepoints}
lifestyledata %>%
  summarise(n_timepoints = n_distinct(year))

lifestyledata %>%
  distinct(year) %>%
  arrange(year)
```

# 2. Transform

## 2a) Create categories for a continuous variable (BMI)

Standard WHO-style cut-points are used here as an example
(Low < 18.5, Medium 18.5–24.9, High ≥ 25). Adjust the breaks/labels to
whatever definition your assignment/brief specifies.

```{r bmi-categories}
lifestyledata <- lifestyledata %>%
  mutate(
    bmi_category = cut(
      bmi,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 18.5, 25, Inf),
      labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
      right = FALSE
    )
  )

# Check the counts in each category
table(lifestyledata$bmi_category, useNA = "ifany")
```

# 3. Summarise

## 3a) Summary table for continuous variables by year

Base R `summary()` for a quick look (matches the Min/1stQ/Median/Mean/3rdQ/Max
style shown in the brief):

```{r base-summary}
summary(lifestyledata$bmi)
summary(lifestyledata$age)
summary(lifestyledata$weight)
```

A tidy summary **by year**, including mean, median, IQR, min and max for
several continuous variables at once:

```{r summary-by-year}
lifestyledata %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    across(
      c(bmi, age, weight),
      list(
        mean   = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        IQR    = ~IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        min    = ~min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
        max    = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
      ),
      .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## 3b) Publication-quality summary table

`gtsummary::tbl_summary()` produces a clean, journal-style table, split by
year, with median (IQR) and range by default:

```{r gtsummary-table}
lifestyledata %>%
  select(year, bmi, age, weight) %>%
  tbl_summary(
    by = year,
    statistic = all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd}); {median} [{p25}, {p75}]; range {min}-{max}",
    missing = "ifany",
    label = list(
      bmi ~ "BMI (kg/m²)",
      age ~ "Age (years)",
      weight ~ "Weight (kg)"
    )
  ) %>%
  add_n() %>%
  modify_header(label ~ "**Variable**") %>%
  modify_caption("**Table 1. Participant characteristics by year**") %>%
  bold_labels()
```

# 4. Visualise

## 4a) Correlation matrix

Select the continuous variables of interest, drop missing values pairwise,
compute the correlation matrix, and plot it.

```{r correlation-matrix}
cont_vars <- lifestyledata %>%
  select(bmi, age, weight) # add more continuous variables as needed, e.g. hba1c, waist

cor_matrix <- cor(cont_vars, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
cor_matrix

corrplot(
  cor_matrix,
  method = "color",
  type = "upper",
  addCoef.col = "black",
  tl.col = "black",
  tl.srt = 45,
  diag = FALSE,
  title = "Correlation matrix of continuous variables",
  mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0)
)
```

An alternative pairwise scatterplot + correlation matrix using `GGally`:

```{r ggpairs}
ggpairs(cont_vars, progress = FALSE) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Interpretation:** Look at the printed `cor_matrix` and the plot above —
report which pairs of variables have |r| > 0.7 (commonly treated as "highly
correlated"), e.g. weight and BMI are often strongly correlated since BMI is
derived directly from weight and height.

## 4a) Distribution plots

Histograms (with density overlay) for several continuous variables at once.
Using `pivot_longer()` lets you facet by variable rather than writing a
separate `ggplot()` call for each one.

```{r distribution-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
lifestyledata %>%
  select(bmi, age, weight) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 30,
                  fill = "steelblue", colour = "white", alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(colour = "darkred", linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Distribution of continuous variables",
       x = NULL, y = "Density")
```

Boxplots are a quick complementary way to check skew/outliers:

```{r distribution-boxplots, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
lifestyledata %>%
  select(bmi, age, weight) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = variable, y = value)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Boxplots of continuous variables", x = NULL, y = NULL)
```

## 4b) Do any variables need transforming?

Check skewness numerically as well as visually — as a rough guide, skewness
> |1| is often considered notably skewed and may benefit from a
transformation (e.g. log2, log10, or square-root) to better approximate a
normal distribution for downstream parametric tests.

```{r skewness}
# install.packages("e1071") if not already installed
library(e1071)

lifestyledata %>%
  summarise(
    across(c(bmi, age, weight), ~ skewness(.x, na.rm = TRUE))
  )
```

If a variable (e.g. `weight` or `bmi`) is notably right-skewed, create a
log-transformed version and compare the distributions:

```{r log-transform, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
lifestyledata <- lifestyledata %>%
  mutate(log2_weight = log2(weight))

# Before vs after, side by side
p1 <- ggplot(lifestyledata, aes(x = weight)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Weight (untransformed)", x = "Weight (kg)")

p2 <- ggplot(lifestyledata, aes(x = log2_weight)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "darkorange", colour = "white") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Weight (log2 transformed)", x = "log2(Weight)")

# install.packages("patchwork") if not already installed
library(patchwork)
p1 + p2
```

**Interpretation:** Report the skewness values, note which variable(s) are
skewed, and comment on whether the log2 transform brings the distribution
closer to symmetric/normal.

## 4c) Boxplot/bar graph of variables against a dependent (grouping) variable

Example using the `bmi_category` created in Section 2a as the grouping
variable, plotted against a continuous outcome (swap `hba1c` for whatever
outcome variable you have, or use `gender`/`sex` instead of `bmi_category`).

```{r boxplot-by-group, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
lifestyledata %>%
  select(bmi_category, age, weight) %>%
  pivot_longer(c(age, weight), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi_category, y = value, fill = bmi_category)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Age and Weight by BMI category",
       x = "BMI category", y = NULL, fill = "BMI category")
```

If your dependent variable is categorical with counts rather than a
continuous spread (e.g. comparing group sizes), a bar graph is more
appropriate:

```{r bargraph-by-group, fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
lifestyledata %>%
  count(bmi_category) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bmi_category, y = n, fill = bmi_category)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Number of observations by BMI category",
       x = "BMI category", y = "Count") +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

## 4d) Longitudinal change plot

Mean (with error bars, e.g. 95% CI or SE) of a variable such as HbA1c across
the three years. Swap `hba1c` below for the actual outcome column name in
your dataset (e.g. `bmi` is used here as a stand-in if HbA1c isn't
available).

```{r longitudinal-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
longitudinal_summary <- lifestyledata %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_val = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_val   = sd(bmi, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(sum(!is.na(bmi))),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(longitudinal_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = mean_val, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = mean_val - se_val, ymax = mean_val + se_val),
                width = 0.1, colour = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Longitudinal change in mean BMI by year",
       x = "Year", y = "Mean BMI (± SE)")
```

For a version showing individual-level trajectories (spaghetti plot) rather
than just the group mean, useful if you want to visualise within-person
change over time:

```{r spaghetti-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=5}
lifestyledata %>%
  filter(id %in% sample(unique(id), 100)) %>%  # subsample for readability
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = bmi, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, colour = "grey40") +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line",
               colour = "darkred", linewidth = 1.2) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "point",
               colour = "darkred", size = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Individual BMI trajectories (sample of 100 participants)\nwith overall mean trend",
       x = "Year", y = "BMI")
```

# 5. Statistical analysis

## 5a) Appropriate statistical test

The right test depends on the type of grouping variable and the number of
groups being compared:

- **Two groups** (e.g. Gender: Male vs Female) → independent-samples
  **t-test** (if the outcome is approximately normal) or **Wilcoxon rank-sum
  test** (if skewed/non-normal, per the checks in 4b).
- **Three or more groups** (e.g. LDL category: Low/Medium/High) → one-way
  **ANOVA** (parametric) or **Kruskal-Wallis test** (non-parametric),
  followed by post-hoc pairwise comparisons if the overall test is
  significant.

First check the assumptions (normality within groups, and homogeneity of
variance for ANOVA):

```{r assumption-checks}
# Normality within each group (Shapiro-Wilk; only reliable up to ~5000 obs)
lifestyledata %>%
  group_by(bmi_category) %>%
  summarise(
    shapiro_p = if (n() >= 3 & n() <= 5000) shapiro.test(age)$p.value else NA_real_
  )

# Homogeneity of variance across groups
car::leveneTest(age ~ bmi_category, data = lifestyledata)
```

**Two-group example (t-test / Wilcoxon):**

```{r ttest-example}
# Example: effect of a two-level grouping variable (e.g. gender) on a
# continuous outcome (e.g. hba1c). Replace `gender` and `hba1c` with your
# actual column names.

# Parametric (if roughly normal, equal variance not assumed by default)
# t.test(hba1c ~ gender, data = lifestyledata)

# Non-parametric alternative
# wilcox.test(hba1c ~ gender, data = lifestyledata)
```

**Three-group example (ANOVA / Kruskal-Wallis) using `bmi_category`:**

```{r anova-example}
# Parametric: one-way ANOVA
anova_model <- aov(age ~ bmi_category, data = lifestyledata)
summary(anova_model)

# Post-hoc pairwise comparisons if ANOVA is significant
TukeyHSD(anova_model)

# Non-parametric alternative: Kruskal-Wallis
kruskal.test(age ~ bmi_category, data = lifestyledata)
```

**Interpretation:** Report the test statistic, degrees of freedom (for
t-test/ANOVA), and p-value. State whether the result is statistically
significant at alpha = 0.05, and relate the effect back to the research
question (e.g. "Age differed significantly across BMI categories,
F(2, N) = X, p = Y").
